Ana, can I ask you something personal? I am thinking of doing what you did, and everyone in my family says I am being reckless.
They said exactly the same to me. What is actually stopping you?
Second thoughts. Every single week. How did you know it was the right moment?
I did not know. I was sitting in traffic on a Tuesday, the avenue was completely gridlocked, and something just snapped.
So it happened on a whim, then.
It looked like a whim. It was not. I spent four months doing the numbers, and my brother tried to talk me out of it the entire time.
And did anybody tell you that you were burning your bridges?
Everybody. They were wrong. I handed in my notice, I went through with it, and it was the turning point of my life.

I can tell you the exact date, which people always find slightly odd. It was the fourteenth of March, and I was sitting in my car on the same road I sat on every single morning of my working life. Completely gridlocked. Nothing was moving in either direction. The radio was playing something cheerful, which did not help at all. And I looked down at the clock and worked out that I had been in that car for fifty five minutes and had travelled about a mile and a half. That was the last straw, honestly. It was not the worst morning I had ever had. It was simply the morning where something snapped. I did nothing reckless, you understand. I drove to the office, I sat through three meetings, and I went home. But that evening I told my wife, and six weeks later I handed in my notice. My mother tried very hard to talk me out of it.

Everybody talks about the moment of deciding. Nobody talks about the eight months afterwards, and that is where the difficulty actually lives. I decided on a Sunday, in about four minutes, while I was washing up. It felt wonderful. And then for the rest of that year I had second thoughts roughly every second week. My brother told me I was burning my bridges. A colleague said I was being reckless at forty three. I very nearly did not go through with it. Twice. What finally helped was something my grandmother said to me. She said, you are not deciding whether to be happy, you are deciding which problems you would rather have. So I chose the new problems. I have never once wanted the old ones back. But I want to be honest with you: it was not a brave decision taken on a whim. It was a frightened decision taken very slowly.

Can I ask what actually made you do it, in the end? There was one Tuesday. I was sitting in traffic and the road had not moved in forty minutes. And that was the moment? That was the last straw, yes. Something just snapped. Did anyone try to stop you? Everybody. My brother spent a month trying to talk me out of it.
